entries.name: The Realist Novel
entries.description: Fiction that seeks a truthful, densely particularised representation of ordinary social and material life.
entries.principle: The realist contract subordinates spectacle to observed detail and probability, treating the texture of the ordinary as sufficient subject. What is load-bearing is fidelity: the sense that this world obeys the same laws as ours, so meaning arises from attention rather than plot machinery.
entries.example: George Eliot's Middlemarch anatomises a provincial town so completely that moral consequence emerges from social pressure alone; Flaubert's Madame Bovary makes free indirect style the instrument of that fidelity.
entries.application: Build significance from accumulated particulars and probable causation, and let a summary of events fail to capture what the observation was for.

entries.name: The Psychological / Interior Novel
entries.description: Narrative whose principal action is mental — perception, memory and feeling rendered from inside.
entries.principle: Here interiority is the plot; the outward event matters only as it registers on a mind. Stream-of-consciousness is one technique within the form, not its definition, and the reference question is whether the sentence enacts the movement of a consciousness rather than reporting it.
entries.example: Woolf's Mrs Dalloway routes a single day through shifting minds so that the party, not the war, becomes the site of meaning; Dostoevsky's Crime and Punishment makes guilt a pressure felt from within before it is a plot.
entries.application: Locate the action in the gap between what a character perceives and what is happening, and trust the reader to assemble the outer world from inner traces.

entries.name: Autofiction / Autobiographical Novel
entries.description: Fiction that foregrounds the author's own life and name while retaining fictional licence.
entries.principle: The form holds the referential pact and the fictional pact in deliberate tension, so the reader is never permitted to settle whether this happened. That undecidability is the meaning, distinguishing autofiction from memoir, whose truth-claim is primary.
entries.example: Knausgård's My Struggle stakes everything on the name and the granular real, while Cusk's Outline hollows the narrating self almost to absence; both make the pact itself the subject.
entries.application: Signal the referential frame plainly, then exploit the licence, so the friction between confession and invention does the work.

entries.name: Bildungsroman
entries.description: The novel of formation, tracing a protagonist's education toward integration into or rupture with society.
entries.principle: The archetype is formally self-conscious about growth as a shaped arc, its telos the negotiation between self and social order. It differs from loose coming-of-age by that integration pressure and its German-critical inheritance.
entries.example: Goethe's Wilhelm Meister's Apprenticeship set the template of vocation and society; Ferrante's My Brilliant Friend reopens it as two girls' formation is bent by class, gender and place.
entries.application: Make the world a school and the ending a settlement, whether reconciliation or refusal, so the reader reads the whole as a curriculum.

entries.name: Künstlerroman
entries.description: A bildungsroman subtype whose subject's formation is specifically toward artistic vocation.
entries.principle: The differentia is destination: the protagonist grows not into society but into art, so the book's form often rehearses the aesthetic it argues for. The making of the artist and the making of the work become the same question.
entries.example: Joyce's A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man lets its prose mature with Stephen, style enacting vocation; Cather's The Song of the Lark tracks a singer's ascent as a costing of ordinary life.
entries.application: Let the growth of craft be visible in the sentences, so form dramatises the vocation the plot describes.

entries.name: Campus / Academic Novel
entries.description: Satire or drama set in the university, using the closed academic world to anatomise intellect and status.
entries.principle: The campus functions as microcosm, a sealed society where ideas, vanity and institutional folly can be examined at pressure. It is literary when the setting is a lens on manners and thought rather than a backdrop for a mystery.
entries.example: Amis's Lucky Jim turns provincial academic status-anxiety into comedy; Nabokov's Pnin uses the émigré scholar to make displacement, not tenure, the true subject.
entries.application: Treat the institution as a moral theatre in miniature and let its rituals expose what its members will not say.

entries.name: State-of-the-Nation / Social-Panorama Novel
entries.description: Wide-angle fiction mapping a whole society across classes and institutions at a historical moment.
entries.principle: The contract is breadth: the book earns its meaning by holding many social strata in one frame, so structure itself makes an argument about how a society coheres or fails to. It differs from the domestic novel by canvas and from the historical novel by its present-tense stake.
entries.example: Dickens's Bleak House binds Chancery to the slum through a single fog; Zadie Smith's White Teeth braids immigrant London across generations to portray a nation remaking itself.
entries.application: Choose a connective device — an institution, a lawsuit, a place — that lets disparate lives touch, and let the pattern of connection carry the claim.

entries.name: The Domestic Novel
entries.description: Fiction centred on household, marriage and family, treating the private sphere as sufficient moral theatre.
entries.principle: The scale is the household, and the wager is that ordinary domestic life holds moral stakes as large as any war. It is literary when interiority and form are load-bearing rather than when family conflict is merely plotted as melodrama.
entries.example: Austen's Emma makes a small society's marriages a rigorous ethics of perception; Robinson's Gilead turns a dying father's letter to his son into a theology of the ordinary.
entries.application: Keep the frame small and the attention total, so a marriage or a kitchen carries the weight a battlefield would elsewhere.

entries.name: The Novel of Ideas
entries.description: Fiction in which the dramatisation and collision of ideas is the primary engine.
entries.principle: Characters partly serve as vehicles for argument, but the ideas remain embodied in scene and consciousness rather than delivered as essay. The test is whether the thought is lived by someone, distinguishing the form from the essay-novel's discursive register.
entries.example: Mann's The Magic Mountain stages a sanatorium as a debating chamber where illness makes philosophy urgent; Dostoevsky's The Brothers Karamazov lets faith and doubt fight through fully realised brothers.
entries.application: Give each idea a body that will suffer for it, so argument reaches the reader as drama rather than lecture.

entries.name: The Epistolary Novel
entries.description: Narrative told wholly or largely through documents — letters, diaries, and now emails or texts.
entries.principle: The form is a container whose mediation is the meaning: every event arrives already written by an interested hand, so unreliability, delay and address become structural. What a summary destroys is precisely the sense of the document as an act.
entries.example: Laclos's Les Liaisons dangereuses weaponises the letter as seduction and evidence at once; Walker's The Color Purple makes address to God and to a lost sister the very shape of a recovered voice.
entries.application: Choose documents that a character would plausibly write, and let the gaps between them — what is unsent, misread, or late — carry the story.

entries.name: The Literary Short Story
entries.description: Compressed prose fiction organised for a single sitting's unity of effect.
entries.principle: The form prizes implication, image and the unsaid over resolution, turning on a shift of understanding rather than a settled plot. It is protected story-first territory: the story that refuses novelistic expansion, closing open or closed but always by a turn the summary cannot hold.
entries.example: Chekhov's The Lady with the Dog withholds resolution so the change is entirely interior; O'Connor's A Good Man Is Hard to Find drives to a single violent instant of grace.
entries.application: Aim every element at one effect and locate the story's whole meaning in a turn, then stop before the novel's machinery can start.

entries.name: The Short-Story Cycle / Linked Collection
entries.description: A book of stories that coheres as a unit through recurring place, character or theme.
entries.principle: The cycle occupies the ground between collection and novel, absorbing the novel-in-stories: each piece stands alone, yet the whole means more than its parts through accretion and echo. The differentia is unity across discrete, self-sufficient stories rather than continuous plot.
entries.example: Anderson's Winesburg, Ohio binds a town's grotesques through a single wandering witness; Strout's Olive Kitteridge lets a difficult woman surface across thirteen stories to compose a life.
entries.application: Let each story satisfy alone, then arrange recurrence so the gaps between them build a shape no single story states.

entries.name: The Novella
entries.description: Prose fiction of intermediate length exploiting concentration and single-arc intensity.
entries.principle: The novella is a form of pressure, long enough for development but short enough to hold one arc at full tension. It is literary when the compression is expressive — a chosen concentration — rather than merely a novel cut short.
entries.example: Conrad's Heart of Darkness sustains a single river journey as a tightening moral descent; Johnson's Train Dreams compresses a labourer's whole century into a taut, luminous span.
entries.application: Commit to one arc and one pressure, using the middle length to intensify rather than to widen.

entries.name: The Fragmentary / Collage Novel
entries.description: Fiction built from discontinuous fragments, lists, footnotes or juxtaposed materials.
entries.principle: Discontinuity is the form: the reader must perform the assembly the book withholds, so meaning lives in the white space between parts. The arrangement itself argues that experience does not come pre-connected.
entries.example: Offill's Dept. of Speculation renders a marriage as swept-together shards of thought; Markson's Wittgenstein's Mistress builds an entire mind and cosmos from isolated declarative facts.
entries.application: Cut the connective tissue deliberately and trust juxtaposition, so the reader's act of joining fragments becomes the experience.

entries.name: Historiographic Metafiction
entries.description: Fiction that foregrounds its own constructedness while re-narrating history and how the past is known.
entries.principle: The form re-tells history while thematising the telling, questioning who narrates the past and on what authority. It differs from the historical novel proper, which does not turn to examine its own historiography — a boundary the historical pack co-holds.
entries.example: Rushdie's Midnight's Children ties a narrator's faulty memory to a nation's birth and admits its own errors; Fowles's The French Lieutenant's Woman intrudes to offer rival endings and expose the Victorian frame.
entries.application: Let the narrator's authority over the past be visibly in question, so the reader feels history being assembled rather than received.

entries.name: The Postcolonial Novel
entries.description: Fiction that writes from, against or after empire, remaking language and form from the margins.
entries.principle: The form is defined by its stance toward empire, not by geography, contesting colonial narrative and reshaping the inherited language to carry an unadmitted world. It overlaps diaspora but foregrounds the colony-metropole relation.
entries.example: Achebe's Things Fall Apart narrates an Igbo world on its own terms so that conquest reads as loss, not progress; Salih's Season of Migration to the North turns the imperial gaze back on the metropole.
entries.application: Make form and idiom themselves the argument, so the way the book speaks contests the empire it depicts.

entries.name: The Immigrant / Diaspora Novel
entries.description: Fiction of migration, displacement and hyphenated identity, dwelling between origin and adopted worlds.
entries.principle: The axis is belonging: the book lives in the gap between where a character comes from and where they now stand, making the unresolved double allegiance its subject. It differs from the postcolonial novel, which centres empire, though the two frequently coincide.
entries.example: Lahiri's The Namesake makes a mispronounced name the whole weight of a second-generation life; Adichie's Americanah reads race and return across two continents through an outsider's exacting eye.
entries.application: Locate meaning in the friction of two worlds, letting small dislocations of language, food or naming carry the larger rupture.

entries.name: The Encyclopedic / "Difficult" Novel
entries.description: Maximalist fiction attempting to encompass a whole field of knowledge or a civilisation.
entries.principle: The ambition is scale and difficulty: the book takes in an entire domain and demands the reader's labour as part of its meaning. Its allusiveness and length are not obstacles to the point but the medium of it.
entries.example: Pynchon's Gravity's Rainbow absorbs war, science and paranoia into one vast weave; Bolaño's 2666 sets five books against a border's unending murders to exhaust a century's violence.
entries.application: Let reach and demand be intentional, so the difficulty enacts the totality the book is trying to hold.

entries.name: The Lyric / Prose-Poetic Novel
entries.description: Fiction whose sentence-music, image and rhythm carry as much meaning as event.
entries.principle: Here the prose approaches poetry, and language is the primary bearer of meaning — the pack's core claim in its purest form. What a plot summary destroys is nearly everything, because the significance lives in cadence and figure.
entries.example: Woolf's The Waves dissolves character into six voices' rhythmic soliloquies; Ondaatje's The English Patient lets image and lyric interval, not chronology, hold the war together.
entries.application: Write so the sentence's sound and image do the work event usually does, and measure success by what survives paraphrase.

entries.name: The Political Novel
entries.description: Fiction in which power, ideology, revolution or the state is the central subject and pressure on private life.
entries.principle: Politics is both subject and structuring force, bearing down on intimate life until the two cannot be separated. It differs from the social panorama by its focus on power and ideology rather than social breadth.
entries.example: Conrad's Nostromo makes silver and revolution corrode every private motive in an invented republic; Gordimer's Burger's Daughter tracks a daughter's reluctant inheritance of the anti-apartheid struggle.
entries.application: Push the political onto the personal until a private choice becomes an ideological one, and let that pressure structure the book.

entries.name: The Regional / Place Novel
entries.description: Fiction rooted so deeply in a specific locale that place functions as character.
entries.principle: Place is the determinant, shaping idiom, values and fate so that the story could not be lifted elsewhere. It differs from the social panorama, whose canvas is society at large rather than a single ground.
entries.example: Faulkner's Absalom, Absalom! makes Yoknapatawpha's soil and history inescapable to every fate within it; Haruf's Plainsong lets a plain Colorado town set the plain register of its own telling.
entries.application: Let the locale shape voice, causation and limit, so removing the place would unmake the book.

entries.name: The Coming-of-Age Novel
entries.description: The broad story of growing up — first experience, loss of innocence, the threshold to adulthood.
entries.principle: Looser and less German-inflected than the bildungsroman, it carries no obligatory social-integration telos, resting on the threshold moment itself. The pack keeps it distinct so both the strict and the popular forms of formation can be carded.
entries.example: Salinger's The Catcher in the Rye holds its narrator at the very edge of adulthood and refuses to push him over; Cisneros's The House on Mango Street builds a girlhood from vignettes on a single street.
entries.application: Centre a threshold rather than a settlement, and let voice register the distance between the child seeing and the adult telling.

entries.name: The Domestic Epic / Multigenerational Saga
entries.description: Family history across generations used as a lens on historical and social change.
entries.principle: The differentia is time-span: the household extended through generations becomes an instrument for reading how history moves through private life. It is literary when form and consciousness carry the weight rather than commercial family melodrama.
entries.example: Mann's Buddenbrooks charts a merchant family's decline as an era's, illness and refinement rising together; García Márquez's One Hundred Years of Solitude folds a century of Macondo into cyclical, mythic time.
entries.application: Use recurrence and inheritance across generations to make private change legible as historical change.

entries.name: The Essay-Novel
entries.description: Fiction incorporating sustained essayistic passages as an integral formal register.
entries.principle: The form blurs novel and essay, delivering discourse essayistically rather than only dramatising it in scene. That distinguishes it from the novel of ideas, where thought stays embodied in character and event.
entries.example: Kundera's The Unbearable Lightness of Being suspends its lovers to reason directly about weight and return; Sebald's The Rings of Saturn drifts from walk to meditation until narration and essay are indistinguishable.
entries.application: Let the discursive voice become a formal instrument in its own right, so the essayistic passages read as part of the fiction's music, not intrusions on it.

entries.name: Literary Science Fiction
entries.description: Speculative fiction whose primary contract is formal and interpretive rather than a genre engine — owned by sf-reference.
entries.principle: This book-type is handed off to the sf-reference pack, which owns the SF craft. SF asks whether the extrapolation is rigorous; literary asks whether prose and consciousness carry meaning the premise alone cannot.
entries.example: Le Guin's The Left Hand of Darkness uses a thought-experiment world to press on gender and love; Atwood's Oryx and Crake makes voice and grief, not the engineered plague, the true weight.
entries.application: When the extrapolation is the point, work in the SF pack; when the manner of telling is load-bearing, hold to the literary contract and hand the world-logic across.

entries.name: Literary Crime
entries.description: Crime fiction whose primary contract is formal and interpretive rather than a puzzle — owned by mystery-crime-thriller-reference.
entries.principle: This book-type is handed off to the mystery-crime-thriller-reference pack, which owns the investigation craft. MCT asks whether the investigation is fair; literary asks whether the crime is the occasion for a study of consciousness or society rather than a puzzle.
entries.example: Dostoevsky's Crime and Punishment abandons the whodunit for the murderer's interior reckoning; Highsmith's The Talented Mr Ripley makes identity and amorality, not detection, the subject.
entries.application: When fair-play detection is the engine, work in the MCT pack; when the crime opens onto mind or society, hold the literary contract and hand the mechanics across.

entries.name: Literary Fantasy
entries.description: Fantastic fiction whose primary contract is formal and figurative rather than a built system — owned by fantasy-reference.
entries.principle: This book-type is handed off to the fantasy-reference pack, which owns the worldbuilding craft. Fantasy asks whether the world coheres as a system; literary asks whether the fantastic is a formal or figurative device rather than a built world.
entries.example: García Márquez's One Hundred Years of Solitude treats the marvellous as ordinary fact for figurative ends; Kafka's The Metamorphosis opens with a transformation it never explains or systematises.
entries.application: When the world must cohere as a working system, work in the fantasy pack; when the fantastic is a trope or figure, hold the literary contract and hand the system across.

entries.name: Literary Horror
entries.description: Fiction of dread whose primary contract is formal and interpretive rather than a fear payload — owned by horror-reference.
entries.principle: This book-type is handed off to the horror-reference pack, which owns the craft of fear. Horror asks what the fear is of; literary asks whether dread is a mode of attention rather than a payload.
entries.example: Jackson's We Have Always Lived in the Castle sustains unease as a study of a warped consciousness; Morrison's Beloved makes a haunting the form of historical grief rather than a scare.
entries.application: When the delivery of fear is the engine, work in the horror pack; when dread is a way of seeing, hold the literary contract and hand the payload across.

entries.name: Literary Romance
entries.description: Fiction of relationship whose primary contract is formal and interpretive rather than a paid-off promise — owned by romance-reference.
entries.principle: This book-type is handed off to the romance-reference pack, which owns the craft of the promise. Romance asks whether the promise is paid; literary asks whether the relationship is the occasion for something the guarantee would foreclose.
entries.example: Ernaux's Simple Passion studies obsession without any reassurance of resolution; Baldwin's Giovanni's Room lets love end in ruin because the subject is shame, not union.
entries.application: When the emotional guarantee is the contract, work in the romance pack; when the relationship opens onto something the guarantee would close off, hold the literary contract and hand the promise across.

entries.name: Literary Historical
entries.description: Fiction set in the past whose primary contract is formal and interpretive rather than a claim about history — owned by historical-reference.
entries.principle: This book-type is handed off to the historical-reference pack, which owns the craft of reconstruction, and co-holds the historiographic-metafiction boundary. Historical asks what claim the book makes about the past; literary asks what prose and consciousness do that faithful reconstruction alone cannot.
entries.example: Mantel's Wolf Hall renders Cromwell's present-tense consciousness so the past is felt from inside; Sebald's Austerlitz lets memory and image, not chronicle, carry the weight of history.
entries.application: When the claim about the past is the point, work in the historical pack; when prose and consciousness exceed reconstruction, hold the literary contract and hand the record across.

entries.category: The Sentence as a Unit of Meaning
entries.name: Syntax as argument
entries.description: The grammar of a sentence performs its interpretive claim rather than merely reporting content.

examples.text: Morrison withholds the grammatical subject and releases it late, so the sentence's own deferral enacts the theme of an inheritance claimed only after long delay.
James loads each clause with qualification and suspension so the syntax itself argues that Strether's perception is always outrunning his certainty.
Brown's uniform subject-verb-object sentences carry no load beyond information, so the grammar does nothing a plot paraphrase would not.

entries.category: The Sentence as a Unit of Meaning
entries.name: The long, accretive sentence
entries.description: Maximal syntax that accumulates clauses to enact a mind under pressure, not merely to postpone the period.

examples.text: Faulkner's sentences pile subordination on subordination so the reader feels the past being dredged up faster than it can be ordered.
Sebald lets a single sentence drift from a walk to a genocide to a silkworm, and the drift is the argument that everything connects by decay.
Roberts extends sentences by heaping clauses that add incident without architecture, so length postpones the period without accruing meaning.

entries.category: The Sentence as a Unit of Meaning
entries.name: The fragment as a made effect
entries.description: The minimal or broken sentence used deliberately for rupture and the withheld connective, not as a nervous tic.

examples.text: Johnson snaps syntax mid-thought so the gaps between fragments carry the addict-narrator's blackouts as form rather than report.
Adler builds from discrete short paragraphs whose refusal to connect is itself the portrait of a fractured urban attention.

examples.work: All the Light We Cannot See
examples.text: Doerr's clipped short sentences recur so regularly that the fragmentation becomes a decorative cadence rather than a made rupture.

entries.category: The Sentence as a Unit of Meaning
entries.name: Parataxis and hypotaxis as worldview
entries.description: The choice between coordinating and subordinating syntax as a claim about whether the world arrives flat-and-equal or ranked-and-conditional.

examples.text: Hemingway's flat coordination places trauma and weather on the same grammatical level, so the parataxis withholds the ranking the reader expects.
James's dense subordination makes every perception conditional on another, so the hypotaxis argues that nothing is known except in relation.
Kerouac's chained "and" coordination becomes a house style rather than a chosen worldview, so the parataxis reads as momentum without discrimination.

entries.category: The Sentence as a Unit of Meaning
entries.name: The periodic sentence
entries.description: A sentence that suspends its meaning until a final clause, generating suspense inside its own span.

examples.work: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
examples.text: Joyce delays the resolving verb until the whole ascending clause lands on it, so the sentence itself performs an epiphany.
Nabokov holds the reader across cascading appositives before the payoff clause, and the suspension seduces the reader into the narrator's rhythm before his crime.
Rand's long suspended sentences arrive at a final clause that only restates a thesis, so the periodic delay pays off in lecture rather than revelation.

entries.category: The Sentence as a Unit of Meaning
entries.name: Rhythm and cadence
entries.description: Prose measured as sound, whose pulse makes it memorable — and which fails when music drowns sense.

examples.text: Robinson tunes clause length and stress so the prose breathes like water, and the cadence carries the book's argument about transience below the level of statement.
Woolf's soliloquies scan almost as verse, the recurring beat binding six voices into one tidal rhythm.
Waller reaches for lyrical cadence so insistently that the rhythm runs on after the sense has emptied, music without a subject.

entries.category: The Sentence as a Unit of Meaning
entries.name: Plainness as an achieved effect
entries.description: The transparent sentence as a deliberate, charged instrument, distinct from flatness that is merely thin.

examples.work: The Old Man and the Sea
examples.text: Hemingway strips the sentence to declarative bone so the plainness itself becomes charged, each simple statement bearing more than it says.
Johnson renders a labourer's century in plain, exact sentences whose restraint makes the few lyric moments detonate.
James's plain sentences are thin rather than chosen, offering clarity that reveals no pressure beneath the surface.

entries.category: The Sentence as a Unit of Meaning
entries.name: The sentence that enacts what it describes
entries.description: Form mirroring content so the sentence performs its subject rather than only naming it.

examples.text: Woolf's sentences swell and subside with the movement of the day, so the syntax rises and settles as consciousness itself does.
Joyce's "Sirens" episode arranges its sentences as musical phrasing, the prose imitating the fugue it describes without collapsing into noise.
Foer pushes typographic and syntactic mimicry until the device becomes cute, the sentence performing itself rather than its grief.

entries.category: The Sentence as a Unit of Meaning
entries.name: Repetition and anaphora as structure
entries.description: Recurrence used as incantation and structural spine, the refrain accruing meaning on each return rather than filling space.

examples.text: Morrison repeats phrases across the "sixty million and more" until the refrain becomes a rite, each recurrence deepening rather than restating.
Vonnegut's "So it goes" after every death accretes into an argument about numbness and mortality that no single instance could make.
Yanagihara repeats scenes of suffering so relentlessly that the anaphora of pain hectors rather than accrues, numbing the reader it means to move.

entries.category: The Sentence as a Unit of Meaning
entries.name: Diction and the register of a single word
entries.description: Word choice as the smallest unit of stance, the exact word revealing a narrator or breaking a tone.

examples.text: Nabokov's narrator betrays himself in a single caressing adjective, so diction discloses the predator the prose is trying to charm past.
Mantel chooses period-plausible words that never announce their research, so the register itself keeps Cromwell's mind inside its own century.
Meyer reaches for ornamental adjectives that break the plain teenage register, so the diction fights the voice it is meant to build.

entries.name: Free indirect discourse
entries.description: Narration bending into a character's idiom without quotation marks or attribution, fusing narratorial and character voice.

examples.text: Austen lets the narration slide into Emma's self-flattering reasoning so seamlessly that the reader adopts her errors and is corrected alongside her, irony delivered at zero distance.
Flaubert dissolves the boundary between report and Emma Bovary's romantic clichés, so the reader inhabits and judges her longing in the same clause.
Smith's narration slides among so many characters' idioms that no single anchoring voice holds, and the free indirect style loses the tension between narrator and mind.

entries.name: Close third and its slippage
entries.description: The distance dial inside third person — controlled nearness and pull-back, distinct from uncontrolled head-hopping.

examples.text: Mantel's roving "he" stays welded to Cromwell yet can pull back a half-step to note his own performance, distance managed to the inch.
Franzen moves deep inside each family member in turn and modulates the closeness by whole degrees, never inside two heads in one scene.
Rowling's third person hops between characters within single scenes, so proximity that should feel intimate reads instead as uncontrolled drift.

entries.name: First person and the problem of narration
entries.description: The teller made part of the tale — who is speaking, and why now — rather than an "I" that is only a camera.

examples.text: Dickens splits the older Pip narrating from the younger Pip acting, so the gap between them becomes the novel's moral instrument.
Barnes makes the narrator's motive for telling — self-justification — the very thing the reader must read around.
Meyer's first person functions as a camera with an "I" attached, recording events without a shaping presence that would make the telling matter.

entries.name: Unreliable narration
entries.description: The gap between what a narrator asserts and what the reader is led to infer, making us read past the teller.

examples.text: Ishiguro's butler misreads his own life so consistently that his composure becomes the evidence of everything he cannot admit.
Nabokov's annotator commandeers another man's poem, and the reader assembles the truth from the very distortions he cannot suppress.
Flynn's unreliability is sprung as a mid-book trick rather than sustained as inference, so the gap is a reveal to be gasped at, not a way of reading.

entries.name: Second person
entries.description: The "you" pronoun as address, indictment, dissociation — chosen for a reason the narrative earns, not for novelty.

examples.text: McInerney's "you" enacts the narrator's dissociation from his own self-destruction, the pronoun holding him at arm's length from a grief he cannot face.

examples.work: If on a winter's night a traveler
examples.text: Calvino addresses "you, the reader" to make the act of reading the book's actual subject, the pronoun motivated at every turn.
Kepnes anchors the second person in a stalker's address to his victim, but the pronoun serves the hook more than the psychology, its motive thinner than its cleverness.

entries.name: The collective "we"
entries.description: A communal narrator — the town, the group, the chorus — used as a single consciousness that earns its plurality.

examples.text: Eugenides narrates through a "we" of neighbourhood boys whose collective obsession is the point, the plural voice a shared act of memory and failure.
Faulkner's townspeople-"we" gossips and judges as one, the communal voice becoming complicit in the secret it discovers too late.

examples.work: Then We Came to the End
examples.text: Ferris opens with an office "we" but keeps slipping into individually staged scenes, so the plurality is asserted more than it is sustained.

entries.name: Omniscience, roving and hierarchical
entries.description: The narrator who knows all and ranks what is known, providing a moral intelligence above the characters.

examples.text: Eliot's narrator moves among every consciousness in the town and judges each with a sympathy that is itself the novel's moral argument.
Tolstoy shifts from a soldier's terror to the sweep of armies and back, the hierarchy of scale organising a whole theory of history.
Follett uses omniscient access mainly to deliver backstory and intention, so the all-knowing narrator dumps information rather than exercising judgement.

entries.name: The intrusive, essayistic narrator
entries.description: A narrator who comments, digresses, and thinks aloud as a presence in the book — not merely a reporter of events.

examples.text: Sterne's narrator digresses so constitutively that the digression becomes the story, the intrusions enacting the impossibility of telling a life in order.
Fielding opens each book with an essay and addresses the reader as an equal, the intruding voice making the narration itself a companionable argument.
Rand's narrator and mouthpieces halt the action to lecture, so authorial intrusion scolds and instructs rather than thinks alongside the reader.

entries.name: The camera-eye, behaviourist exterior
entries.description: A refusal of interiority in which meaning is inferred entirely from surface — dialogue, gesture, object.

examples.text: Hemingway reports only speech and setting around an unnamed decision, so the whole weight of the abortion is inferred from what the surface withholds.
Hemingway stages the scene from outside, letting the flat exterior of the diner carry a dread no interior access could sharpen.
Ellis withholds interiority to signal anomie, but the flat surface hides no inferable depth, so the exteriority becomes opacity that conceals nothing.

entries.name: Multiple, rotating point of view
entries.description: The polyphonic novel that renders truth as the sum of partial, differentiated views.

examples.text: Faulkner gives each family member a distinct idiom and blind spot, so the mother's coffin is assembled from fifteen incompatible consciousnesses.

examples.work: A Visit from the Goon Squad
examples.text: Egan rotates through a network of lives in radically different forms, each chapter's voice and mode chosen to fit the character it inhabits.
Stockett rotates three narrators whose voices flatten toward a single register, so the rotation multiplies perspective without multiplying difference.

entries.name: The unreliable frame and nested telling
entries.description: A narrator-of-a-narrator structure that puts the act of telling itself in question.

examples.text: Brontë filters the story through Lockwood hearing it from Nelly, so every passion reaches the reader twice-mediated and therefore suspect.
Shelley nests the creature's account inside Victor's inside Walton's letters, the frames making the reader weigh who is trusted with sympathy.
Mitchell nests six narratives inside one another, but the outer frames add structural layering more than they interrogate the reliability of any telling.

entries.name: Direct address to the reader in earnest
entries.description: Breaking toward the reader for intimacy, complicity or testimony, distinct from the metafictional wink.

examples.text: Brontë's "Reader, I married him" claims the reader as confidant at the climactic moment, the address converting narration into testimony.
Zusak lets Death narrate and address the reader directly, the confiding voice making mortality companionable rather than abstract.
Sebold's murdered narrator addresses the reader from an afterlife, but the direct appeal flatters and consoles rather than implicates, softening what it touches.

entries.name: Stream of consciousness
entries.description: The near-unpunctuated flow of a mind rendered as syntax dissolves, catching thought before it is tidied into speech.

examples.text: Joyce's closing Molly Bloom episode runs almost without punctuation, the associative surge and repetition catching a mind at the edge of sleep so completely that grammar itself thins toward pure consciousness.
Faulkner renders Benjy's perception without temporal markers, the flow refusing to sort memory from present as an ordered mind would.
Kerouac's celebrated spontaneity is in fact grammatically ordered narration with the pauses removed, so the "flow" is tidy interior monologue wearing the costume of stream.

entries.name: Interior monologue
entries.description: Quoted or unquoted thought that remains grammatical — the character thinking in whole sentences.

examples.text: Woolf lets Mrs Ramsay think in complete, shapely sentences that nonetheless swerve with feeling, monologue that is ordered without being expository.
Dostoevsky's narrator argues with himself in grammatical prose, the monologue dramatising a mind that cannot stop contradicting its own claims.
Hawkins routes plot information through interior monologue, so the character's thoughts mainly tell the reader what to know rather than render a mind at work.

entries.name: Psycho-narration
entries.description: The narrator reporting a consciousness the character could not articulate, reaching beyond the character's own words.

examples.text: James narrates the movements of Strether's awareness in a register finer than Strether could command, giving the reader a mind the man cannot phrase.
Eliot articulates Maggie Tulliver's inchoate feeling in the narrator's own analytic language, naming pressures the girl only suffers.
Hosseini's narrator states emotions flatly, so the reporting of inner life names feelings ("I felt so guilty") instead of rendering the consciousness beneath them.

entries.name: Rendering thought without markers
entries.description: Interior life given with no italics and no "he thought," seeking a seamless fusion of mind and world.

examples.text: Mantel drops thought straight into the narration with no tag, so Cromwell's calculation and the room he stands in occupy one unbroken surface.
Ellmann runs a housewife's thought as a single near-continuous clause without markers, the absence of tags making the whole novel one uninterrupted mind.
Rowling omits thought markers while hopping between characters, so unmarked interiority becomes ambiguous by accident rather than fused by design.

entries.name: Represented perception, the figural
entries.description: The world rendered as filtered through a perceiving mind, the seen visibly shaped by the seer.

examples.text: Woolf gives the same window and sea different colour and meaning depending on whose perception frames them, so the object is inseparable from the perceiver.
Ford filters every scene through Dowell's limited, wounded understanding, so what we see is always what his blindness lets through.

examples.work: All the Light We Cannot See
examples.text: Doerr renders the blind girl's world in exhaustive detail, but the perception is rarely coloured by her particular mind, so the filter changes little of what it passes.

entries.name: Time in the mind, durée
entries.description: Clock time set against felt time — the elastic present of consciousness enacted rather than asserted.

examples.text: Proust dilates a moment of hesitation over pages while a decade passes in a clause, so the prose obeys felt duration rather than the calendar.
Mann lets a sanatorium's early days crawl and its later years blur, the narration slowing and racing to match how illness distorts a patient's sense of time.
Niffenegger dislocates chronology by device and asserts temporal disorientation, but the felt stretch of time is stated by the premise rather than enacted in the prose.

entries.name: The tense of memory
entries.description: Involuntary memory and the past erupting into the present as a live pressure, not mechanical flashback.

examples.text: Proust lets a taste return a lost world unbidden and entire, so memory arrives as an event that happens to the narrator rather than a scene he retrieves.
Sebald lets photographs and stations detonate a suppressed childhood into the present, memory surfacing through image with no flashback machinery.
Hosseini frames the past with signalled flashback devices, so recollection is a labelled retrieval rather than a pressure that breaks in unbidden.

entries.name: Interiority under extremity
entries.description: Consciousness fracturing under trauma, dying or madness, with form breaking as the mind breaks.

examples.text: Faulkner lets Benjy's section collapse chronology and cause because his mind cannot hold them, the broken form motivated entirely by the broken consciousness.
Plath tightens and flattens the narration as Esther's depression closes in, the prose's constriction enacting the illness from inside.
Foer substitutes disordered typography — blank pages, overprinting — for a disordered mind, so the chaos sits on the page without arising from the consciousness.

entries.name: The divided, doubled consciousness
entries.description: The self observing the self — a mind that watches its own workings.

examples.text: Dostoevsky's narrator narrates and simultaneously despises his own narration, the split producing a consciousness caught in the act of watching itself.
Cusk's narrator relentlessly analyses her own motives as she reports them, so the telling is doubled by a self that will not stop interpreting itself.
Rand stages self-analysis that is really the author's argument in the character's mouth, so introspection becomes op-ed rather than a mind observing itself.

entries.name: Collective, distributed consciousness
entries.description: A consciousness that is more than one mind — awareness rendered as a social field.

examples.text: Conrad diffuses awareness across an invented town so that the silver mine's meaning is held by no single mind but by the collective it corrupts.
Eugenides makes the boys' pooled recollection a single distributed mind, the "we" thinking thoughts no member could think alone.
Smith cross-cuts several London consciousnesses but never fuses them into one field, so the intended distribution reads as separate minds side by side.

entries.name: The reflector character
entries.description: A central intelligence — one mind used as the novel's sole lens, knowledge limited to it on principle.

examples.text: James restricts the entire adult drama to a child's partial comprehension, so the novel's meaning lives in the gap between what Maisie registers and what she cannot yet name.
James routes the second half through the Princess's dawning awareness, holding the reader to exactly what one consciousness can reach.
Brown's central mind conveniently perceives whatever each plot beat requires, so the reflector is a lens that sees on demand rather than on principle.

entries.name: Free indirect thought versus speech
entries.description: Interior free indirect discourse — a character's private reasoning given in its own idiom without the tag, pointing irony and sympathy at the mind itself.

examples.text: Austen slips into Anne Elliot's suppressed reasoning without attribution, so the reader feels her restraint from inside while the narration quietly judges it.
Forster lets the narration take on each character's private logic in turn, the shifts of idiom aiming sympathy and irony at their reasoning rather than their speech.
Franzen's figural passages rarely shift register from the surrounding narration, so the interior free indirect voice is hard to distinguish from ordinary report.

entries.name: The vernacular, dialect voice
entries.description: Nonstandard speech carried as narration — a voice the standard register cannot hold.

examples.text: Twain sustains a boy's untutored idiom across a whole book, and the vernacular carries a moral clarity the standard register would have flattened.
Hurston frames a lyrical standard narration around richly rendered speech, the two registers together making a voice neither could make alone.
Stowe renders enslaved characters' speech in heavy eye-dialect that tips toward spectacle, so the transcription condescends to the voices it means to honour.

entries.name: The demotic, maximal voice
entries.description: A torrential, comic, hyperbolic first person whose excess is the engine — provided it modulates.

examples.text: Roth pitches the whole novel as a howling confession to an analyst, the maximal voice modulating between comedy and anguish so the excess never flattens.
Toole's Ignatius bloviates in mock-scholastic grandeur, the hyperbolic register calibrated so that its absurdity keeps revealing his delusion.
Palahniuk sustains a torrential first person at one pitch, so the motormouth voice mistakes loudness for vitality and never modulates.

entries.name: The flat affect, deadpan voice
entries.description: A voice that under-reacts, generating estrangement or irony through the tension between event and tone.

examples.text: Camus reports a mother's funeral and a killing in the same affectless register, the flatness estranging the reader into the moral question the narrator will not ask.
Melville keeps the narration mild and mannerly against Bartleby's escalating refusal, the deadpan making the abyss more disquieting.
Murata's narrator describes social rituals with a manual's neutrality, the flat affect turning ordinary life strange and quietly indicting it.
Ellis flattens the narration to signal numbness, but with no counterweight of event the tone produces affectless writing rather than a charged deadpan.

entries.name: Irony and tone
entries.description: The say-one-mean-another register that holds doubled meaning in a single voice.

examples.text: Austen's opening about a single man in want of a wife means its opposite, and the whole book sustains that doubled register with sympathy intact.
Waugh narrates catastrophe in a cool social register, the irony letting horror and comedy occupy the same sentence.
Ellis aims for satiric irony but lets the register curdle toward the contempt it depicts, so the doubled meaning collapses into the surface it means to mock.

entries.name: The ventriloquised, persona voice
entries.description: A narrator emphatically not the author — a fully invented idiolect that never leaks.

examples.text: Burgess builds Alex's Nadsat so completely that the invented slang becomes the moral texture of the book, the persona sealed against the author's own diction.
Beatty sustains a satirical narrator whose riffing idiom is entirely his own, the persona's logic driving the book's argument.
Pierre's teenage narrator repeatedly slides into an authorial cleverness his character could not own, so the ventriloquism leaks.

entries.name: The essayistic voice
entries.description: A narrator who thinks in argument, rendering ideas as voice without letting the essay swallow the fiction.

examples.text: Cusk builds a narrator who is almost pure listening intelligence, the essayistic reflection becoming the book's action rather than an interruption of it.
Kundera lets the narrator reason directly about weight and return, the argument woven so tightly into the lovers that thought reads as voice.
Tartt closes with pages of philosophising that stall the fiction, the essayism arriving as a lecture bolted onto the story rather than arising from it.

entries.name: Voice built from constraint and idiolect
entries.description: An invented language-system — a degraded, future or other English that means through its own rules.

examples.text: Hoban builds a post-collapse English whose battered spelling and grammar consistently encode a ruined civilisation, the idiolect meaning at every level.
Mitchell's "Sloosha's Crossin'" section sustains a future creole with internal consistency, the degraded language carrying the history that produced it.
Foer's Alex narrates in comically mangled English that is funny but rule-inconsistent, so the idiolect is an effect rather than a system.

entries.name: Code-switching, the multilingual voice
entries.description: Two languages held in one register, rendering the bilingual mind on the page.

examples.work: The Brief Wondrous Life of Oscar Wao
examples.text: Díaz braids Spanish, English and geek argot without translation, so the code-switching enacts a diasporic mind that lives across all three at once.
Cisneros lets Spanish inhabit the English rhythm rather than sit beside it, the switching mapping a border consciousness.
Esquivel sprinkles untranslated tokens mostly for local colour, so the second language garnishes the prose rather than structuring a bilingual mind.

entries.name: The child's voice, the restricted narrator
entries.description: A limited vocabulary used as a lens, the world seen through a genuinely constrained frame.

examples.text: Donoghue holds a five-year-old's vocabulary and cosmology with total discipline, so captivity is rendered through the only frame the child possesses.

examples.work: The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time
examples.text: Haddon builds a narrator whose literal, systematising mind reshapes every event, the restriction becoming the book's way of seeing.
Sebold's murdered child narrates with an omniscience and articulacy beyond the frame, so the restricted voice becomes an adult sensibility wearing a child's mask.

entries.name: Tonal control across a long work
entries.description: Holding or deliberately modulating a chosen register at novel length without slipping out of key.

examples.text: Williams sustains a grave, plain register across a whole quiet life, never once letting sentiment or irony break the key he has chosen.
Ishiguro maintains the butler's decorous diction from first page to last, the unbroken register itself the measure of his repression.
Tartt's register drifts across the book's length, tightening and loosening between thriller pace and lyric reverie without a governing control.

entries.name: Non-linear structure
entries.description: Chronology broken on purpose so that the order of telling itself carries meaning.

examples.text: Vonnegut unstuck Billy Pilgrim in time so that a firebombing sits beside a zoo, the scrambled order enacting a mind that cannot keep trauma in sequence.
Ondaatje lets image and association, not chronology, govern the sequence, so the war is held together by resonance rather than timeline.
Niffenegger shuffles chronology by mechanism, but a straight timeline would lose little, so the disorder is a premise rather than an interpretive gain.

entries.name: The frame narrative
entries.description: A story about the telling of a story, used for distance, testimony or doubt about the tale.

examples.text: Conrad sets Marlow telling his tale aboard a becalmed yawl, the frame putting the reliability and the cost of the telling permanently in question.
Eco presents the book as a rediscovered manuscript at several removes, the frame layering doubt over every claim the narrative makes.
Kostova opens an elaborate frame of letters and researchers that it never meaningfully pays off, so the outer story is scaffolding left standing.

entries.name: Ellipsis and the load-bearing gap
entries.description: The deliberate omission that makes meaning by what it skips rather than what it stages.

examples.work: A Visit from the Goon Squad
examples.text: Egan jumps across decades between chapters, the unwritten years generating the book's ache of lost time more powerfully than any staged scene could.
Barnes builds the novel around a withheld stretch of the past, the gap forcing a reread once its content finally surfaces.
Nicholls skips a year between chapters, but the omissions tend to cut the scenes that would earn the changes, so the gaps evade rather than mean.

entries.name: The braided, parallel timeline
entries.description: Two eras cut against each other so that they rhyme across time.

examples.text: Cunningham braids three women's days across a century so each illuminates the others, the parallel making a single argument about lives and writing.
Byatt cuts Victorian poets against modern scholars until the two eras interpret one another, the braid becoming the book's mystery and its meaning.
Hannah alternates a wartime past with a framing present that adds little the past has not already said, so the strands run parallel without truly touching.

entries.name: The recursive, looping structure
entries.description: A form that returns on itself to enact obsession or infinity, with meaning at the centre of the loop.

examples.text: Nabokov builds a poem, a commentary, and an index that send the reader circling between them, the loop enacting the annotator's obsessive appropriation.

examples.work: If on a winter's night a traveler
examples.text: Calvino opens ten novels that never finish and folds them back into the reader's own pursuit, the recursion becoming the book's argument about reading.
Danielewski nests footnotes within footnotes into an elaborate maze, but the recursion often resolves into a puzzle to be solved rather than a meaning to be felt.

entries.name: The single effect
entries.description: The short story built to one converging impression — Poe's doctrine of unity, every element bent toward a single charge.

examples.text: Poe subordinates every detail to a single mounting dread of entombment, nothing in the story diverging from its one converging effect.

examples.work: A Good Man Is Hard to Find
examples.text: O'Connor drives the whole story toward one instant of violent grace, so every earlier line proves in retrospect to have served that convergence.
Jackson withholds the story's true subject until a final image that reorganises the placid village around one shock.

examples.work: An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge
examples.text: Bierce builds toward one effect, but that effect depends on a concealment that diffuses the story's unity on any second reading.

entries.name: The turn, the reversal
entries.description: The late pivot — peripeteia or the epiphanic swerve — that reorganises everything before it.

examples.text: Joyce turns a comfortable party into a devastation with the snow and Gretta's memory, the swerve tilting the whole evening into a new meaning.
Chekhov lets a satisfied story of contentment turn on a sudden protest against complacency, the reversal reorganising the tale's apparent moral.
Carver ends on a blind man guiding the narrator's hand, the small turn opening a closed man in a single unforced gesture.
Dahl builds to a neat reversal of the murder weapon, but the twist delivers a punchline rather than deepening what came before.

entries.name: The story cycle
entries.description: A linked collection whose meaning emerges only across the set — the book that is more than its stories.

examples.text: Joyce arranges the stories from childhood to death so that paralysis accumulates into a portrait of a whole city no single story could give.
Anderson binds a town's isolated lives through a recurring witness, the cumulative architecture making the town itself the protagonist.
Strout lets a difficult woman surface at the edge and centre of thirteen stories, so a whole life composes only across the set.
Salinger's collection gathers superb individual stories, but they are assembled rather than cumulative, so the book stays a container, not a cycle.

entries.name: The fragment, collage novel
entries.description: A whole assembled from discrete pieces held together by a gravitational field rather than continuous narrative.

examples.text: Adler builds the book from unlinked paragraphs whose juxtaposition generates a consciousness and a milieu no continuous plot would render.
Offill renders a marriage as swept-together shards of thought and quotation, the white space between fragments doing the emotional work.
Rankine assembles prose fragments, images and incidents into a single accumulating account of racial address, the collage building a pressure no argument could.
Semple assembles emails, notes and reports, but the documents mostly relay plot, so the collage lacks the gravitational field that would make the form necessary.

entries.name: The withheld, delayed disclosure
entries.description: A structure organised around what is kept back, so a late key forces a rereading of everything before it.

examples.text: McEwan withholds the status of the narrative itself until a final revelation reframes the whole novel as an act of guilty authorship.

examples.work: We Need to Talk About Kevin
examples.text: Shriver delays a central fact of the family's catastrophe so that its late arrival forces the reader to reweigh every letter that preceded it.
Martel withholds an alternative account until the close, but the disclosure functions mainly to spring a late reveal rather than to reorganise the book's meaning.

entries.name: The day novel
entries.description: The whole book compressed into a single span, using unity of time to concentrate pressure.

examples.text: McEwan runs a whole novel across one London day, the compression forcing a surgeon's public and private dreads to collide within a single span.
Bellow confines a man's reckoning to a single desperate afternoon, the tight span concentrating a lifetime's failure into hours.
DeLillo compresses events into one day's limousine crawl, but the twenty-four-hour frame feels imposed rather than pressured, so the unity is arbitrary.

entries.name: The overture and prolepsis
entries.description: The ending shown or flagged at the outset, relocating suspense from what happens to how it happens.

examples.text: Agee flags the coming death from the first pages, so the ordinary domestic scenes acquire an unbearable tenderness the reader already mourns.
García Márquez announces the murder in the opening line and spends the book on how a whole town let it happen, suspense relocated entirely to the how.
Eugenides has the narrator disclose the outcome of his condition early, but the flash-forward tends to flatten later scenes rather than charge them.

entries.name: Metaphor at load
entries.description: The figure doing structural rather than decorative work — a metaphor that carries the book's meaning.

examples.text: Roy's images of small things and large laws recur as load-bearing structure, the figures organising the whole book's argument about what history permits.
Morrison makes flight the book's governing metaphor, the figure carrying the theme of escape and abandonment rather than ornamenting it.
Roberts sprays simile across nearly every page, the figures detachable without loss, so metaphor decorates rather than means.

entries.name: The controlling image, the central symbol
entries.description: One image the whole book organises around, accreting meaning across its length rather than being announced.

examples.text: Fitzgerald lets the green light gather longing, class and futility across the book, the symbol earning its final weight through accumulation, not statement.
Melville makes the white whale hold irreconcilable meanings at once, the central symbol resisting the very interpretation the crew demands of it.
Coelho announces and then explains his symbols, so the omens and treasure arrive pre-glossed, the image underlined rather than allowed to accrete.

entries.name: The objective correlative
entries.description: Emotion evoked through an external object or situation rather than named — feeling produced by the thing itself.

examples.text: Joyce lets the snow falling across Ireland carry Gabriel's grief and dissolution, the external image producing an emotion the text never states.
Hemingway attaches loss and dread to the recurring rain, the weather bearing the feeling so the prose need not declare it.
Sparks stages a charged rainstorm and then has the narration explain the emotion it stands for, the object supplied with a gloss that cancels its work.

entries.name: The recurring motif
entries.description: An image that returns and gathers weight, building unity and resonance by repetition that earns its returns.

examples.text: Roy threads recurring images and refrains through shifting time so that each return deepens their charge, the motif binding a fractured chronology.
Morrison lets musical figures and repeated phrases return like a refrain, the motif accruing meaning as a song does across choruses.
Coelho repeats the omen motif at intervals, but each recurrence merely restates it, so the return adds insistence without accrual.

entries.name: Defamiliarisation
entries.description: Rendering the familiar as if seen for the first time, restoring perception of the ordinary.

examples.text: Tolstoy describes an opera through a bewildered Natasha's eyes as painted boards and shouting people, the estrangement exposing the convention we no longer see.
Swift makes human institutions strange by shifting their scale, so familiar politics and pride return to view as absurd for having been made literal.
Danielewski estranges perception through typographic disorientation, but the strangeness often serves itself, offering novelty without the renewed sight the technique promises.

entries.name: Synaesthesia, the cross-sensory image
entries.description: Perception rendered whole by crossing the senses, distinct from sensory confusion passed off as richness.

examples.text: Süskind renders a whole world through smell so precisely that scent acquires colour, weight and morality, the cross-sensory image organising the book.
Saramago builds a sightless world in which sound, touch and smell carry the visual load, the sensory transfer enacting the loss it describes.
Robbins piles cross-sensory imagery so freely that senses blur into one another without control, richness tipping into muddle.

entries.name: The extended conceit
entries.description: A single metaphor developed at length as a way of thinking, held only as far as its tension will bear.

examples.text: Robinson sustains light as a conceit across a dying man's letter, developing it through blessing, memory and grace so the figure becomes an instrument of thought.
Robinson extends water and its transience through the whole book, the sustained figure carrying the argument about impermanence without ever hardening into a slogan.
Bach stretches the flight conceit past its tensile limit into open allegory, the figure flogged until it explains itself out of existence.

entries.name: When the figurative overreaches
entries.description: The anti-card — teaching the ceiling of the figurative by setting restraint against purple excess.

examples.text: Williams withholds ornament almost entirely, so the few images land hard, the restraint demonstrating exactly the ceiling the overwritten sentence breaks through.
Lawrence stacks visionary metaphor so densely in its ecstatic passages that the figures compete and blur, the ambition overrunning the sense it means to intensify.
Waller piles metaphor upon metaphor until the imagery drowns the plain feeling beneath it, the figurative overreaching into unintended parody.

entries.name: Negative capability
entries.description: Holding irresolution without reaching for certainty, so meaning is kept genuinely open rather than merely vague.

examples.text: James balances the ghosts and the governess's delusion so evenly that the text sustains both readings at once, the irresolution held on purpose rather than fudged.

examples.work: We Have Always Lived in the Castle
examples.text: Jackson keeps the reader inside a warped consciousness without ever confirming its judgements, the ambiguity a controlled condition rather than a withheld answer.
Martel offers two stories and asks which the reader prefers, but the openness reads as the author declining to decide, vagueness dressed as depth.

entries.name: The earned open ending
entries.description: A story that ends unresolved on purpose, refusing false resolution, distinct from one that merely stops.

examples.text: Chekhov ends with the lovers facing an unresolvable future, the refusal to conclude honouring a change that has no available ending.
McCarthy closes on a sheriff's dream rather than a reckoning, the withheld resolution enacting the book's claim that no order will arrive.
Franzen brings his family to a stop rather than an open irresolution, the ending halting the narrative without the deliberate suspension a true open ending achieves.

entries.name: The story that ends in silence
entries.description: The story-native open ending — the last image carrying the withheld meaning as the narration falls silent.

examples.text: Hemingway ends on a couple agreeing they are fine while the whole undecided abortion hangs in the withheld space, the final quiet carrying everything the surface refuses to say.
Baldwin closes on the glass of scotch trembling on the piano like a cup of trembling, the last image holding a reconciliation the story declines to state.
Roupenian ends on a final message that gestures toward openness, but the closing image carries little charge, so the silence resolves into flatness rather than pressure.

entries.name: Irony as structure
entries.description: A whole work meaning against its own surface, saying one thing while the structure means its opposite.

examples.text: Ford builds an entire narration whose surface calm systematically means its opposite, the structural irony making the "saddest story" a study in self-deception.
Swift sustains an outrageous argument in an earnest, reasonable register for its full length, the whole meaning against every literal sentence.
Ellis intends a structural irony against consumer culture, but the satire cannot hold its distance and collapses toward the literal atrocity it catalogues.

entries.name: The unreliable, withheld resolution
entries.description: An ending that refuses to confirm what actually happened, making the reader author the meaning.

examples.text: McEwan reveals that the consoling ending was invented, so the novel refuses to confirm what the reader most wants to be true and hands the choice back to them.
James ends on a death that confirms neither reading of the haunting, the withheld resolution forcing the reader to decide what the story was.
Palahniuk retro-explains its events with a late twist, but the ambiguity it opens carries thin stakes, so the unconfirmed resolution reads as a mechanism rather than a demand.

entries.name: The refusal to resolve as a claim
entries.description: The unsaid as the point — omission practised as an ethical or aesthetic statement rather than an evasion.

examples.text: Coetzee withholds judgement and consolation at every turn, the refusal to resolve becoming itself a statement about a society with no available reconciliation.
Endō leaves the meaning of God's silence and the apostasy unresolved, the withholding carrying the theological argument the book will not close.
Ishiguro leaves the fog of forgetting deliberately unlifted, but the refusal reads more as evasion than statement, the unsaid registering as authorial reticence rather than claim.

entries.name: Realism
entries.description: Fiction as a truthful representation of ordinary life.
entries.principle: Represent ordinary life truthfully, favouring the probable over the marvellous and treating the everyday interior as a worthy subject; the means are consistent chronology, verisimilar detail, free indirect narration, and the individuated character set in a specific social world.
entries.example: Middlemarch (George Eliot).
entries.application: The default "transparent" contract most fiction still assumes; a writer inherits it as the baseline against which every departure reads as a choice.

entries.name: Naturalism
entries.description: Character as the product of heredity and environment.
entries.principle: Treat character as determined by heredity, environment and social force and the novel as a quasi-scientific experiment on human specimens; the means are documentary observation, the milieu study, the deterministic plot, and unsparing detail.
entries.example: Germinal (Émile Zola).
entries.application: The engine of the sociological and determinist novel; a writer uses it to make individual fate legible as the output of systems larger than the self.

entries.name: The Reality Effect
entries.description: Realism as a coded convention rather than a window.
entries.principle: Recognise that certain concrete details signify nothing but "this is real," so realism is a rhetoric, not a window; the means are the insignificant texture-detail read as a reality-signal and the analysis of verisimilitude as convention.
entries.example: Roland Barthes's "The Reality Effect" (1968), on Flaubert's barometer.
entries.application: Writers deploy or withhold texture-detail knowingly, aware the concrete particular is a signal that can be turned on or off.

entries.name: Social and Socialist Realism
entries.description: Fiction that depicts and contests society's structures.
entries.principle: Depict society's structures — class, labour, injustice — and, in the socialist-realist program, advance a progressive consciousness; the means are the panoramic ensemble, the representative type, and the condition-of-the-people novel.
entries.example: The Grapes of Wrath (John Steinbeck).
entries.application: The lineage of the state-of-the-nation and protest novel; a writer uses it to make a social system, not a private psyche, the protagonist.

entries.name: Psychological Realism
entries.description: The truest realism is realism of the inner life.
entries.principle: Hold that the truest realism is of the inner life — motive, moral deliberation, the movement of consciousness — not just the social surface; the means are sustained interiority, the reflector character, psycho-narration, and moral analysis.
entries.example: The Portrait of a Lady (Henry James).
entries.application: The interior character-novel that remains literary fiction's core; a writer inherits it whenever the drama is located inside a mind rather than in event.

entries.name: The Realist Inheritance Today
entries.description: Realism as a deliberate choice after the experimental century.
entries.principle: After the experimental century, treat realism as a live choice rather than a naive default — a deliberate contract of clarity and character; the means are chastened omniscience, plain style as an option, and the well-made social novel self-aware of its conventions.
entries.example: Freedom (Jonathan Franzen).
entries.application: A writer practises realism as one option among many, its transparency now a knowing stance rather than an assumed given.

entries.name: Modernism
entries.description: Form made strange in the name of fidelity to experience.
entries.principle: Hold that the old realist contract falsifies experience and that fiction must render consciousness, fracture and the felt texture of time as they actually are; the means are deep interiority, fragmentation, mythic scaffolding, and difficulty embraced as fidelity.
entries.example: Ulysses (James Joyce).
entries.application: The standing licence to make form strange in the name of truth; a writer inherits permission to break the transparent surface when experience demands it.

entries.name: Stream of Consciousness as a Program
entries.description: The mind's pre-verbal flow rendered directly.
entries.principle: Represent the mind's pre-verbal flow directly, before it is tidied into speech; the means are unpunctuated interior flow, associative leaps, and the erosion of the narratorial frame that would otherwise organise thought.
entries.example: Ulysses, the "Penelope" episode (James Joyce).
entries.application: Any deep-interiority technique descends from this; a writer uses it to admit thought that grammar and reported speech cannot carry.

entries.name: The Mythic Method
entries.description: Ordering contemporary chaos against ancient myth.
entries.principle: Order the chaos of the contemporary by running it against ancient myth, so a parallel substructure gives shape to the shapeless present; the means are the sustained classical or mythic scaffolding beneath a modern surface.
entries.example: Ulysses (James Joyce), read against the Odyssey.
entries.application: The parallel-structure and mythic-retelling novel; a writer borrows an old story's architecture to lend a formless present its shape. Term associated with T. S. Eliot's 1923 essay on Ulysses.

entries.name: Imagism into Prose
entries.description: No idea but in things — the hard, exact image.
entries.principle: Prefer the direct, hard, exact image to abstraction and rhetoric, letting the concrete particular carry the idea; the means are compression, distrust of the adjective, and the objective presentation of the thing itself.
entries.example: In Our Time (Ernest Hemingway).
entries.application: The minimalist, image-first sentence; a writer inherits the discipline of showing a charged object rather than naming the abstraction behind it.

entries.name: The Objective Correlative as Doctrine
entries.description: Emotion evoked through an external object, never stated.
entries.principle: Evoke emotion through an external set of objects or events rather than stating it, so the feeling is produced by the thing; the means are the charged object, the withheld emotion, and indirection.
entries.example: "The Dead" (James Joyce), where the falling snow carries the grief.
entries.application: The workshop maxim "show the feeling in the thing." The term is commonly credited to T. S. Eliot's popularisation, though it predates him; a writer treats it as a working rule, not a proven origin.

entries.name: Impersonality
entries.description: The author refined out of the work.
entries.principle: Treat the artist's mind as a catalyst and art as an escape from personality, so the author is refined out of the work; the means are the effaced narrator, dramatic objectivity, and the seemingly invisible author.
entries.example: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (James Joyce), whose artist stands "paring his fingernails."
entries.application: The impersonal close-third and camera-eye. The ideal is variously associated with Flaubert, Eliot and Joyce; a writer inherits the effect without owing it to a single source.

entries.name: The Modernist Fragment
entries.description: A broken world shown truthfully only in broken form.
entries.principle: Hold that a broken world can be shown truthfully only in broken form, shoring fragments against ruin; the means are collage, juxtaposition, the missing connective, and discontinuity treated as meaning rather than defect.
entries.example: The Sound and the Fury (William Faulkner).
entries.application: The collage and fragment novel; a writer uses discontinuity itself as an argument that the whole cannot be made continuous.

entries.name: Late Modernism
entries.description: Modernist method pushed toward silence.
entries.principle: Push modernism's methods toward exhaustion or minimalism, rendering consciousness until language thins toward silence; the means are extreme interiority, reduction, and the voice stripped to a murmur.
entries.example: The Unnamable (Samuel Beckett).
entries.application: The reductive, voice-only novel and the bridge to postmodernism; a writer inherits the option of subtracting world and event until only a speaking pressure remains.

entries.name: Postmodernism
entries.description: Fiction foregrounding its own artifice and instability.
entries.principle: Hold that there is no innocent realism and no stable master-narrative, so fiction should foreground its own artifice, play and constructedness; the means are pastiche, irony, metafiction, unreliable frames, and the mixing of registers.
entries.example: The Crying of Lot 49 (Thomas Pynchon).
entries.application: The self-aware, playful, unstable contract; a writer inherits permission to let the novel admit and exploit its own made-ness.

entries.name: Metafiction
entries.description: Fiction that examines its own status as fiction.
entries.principle: Have fiction openly examine its own status as fiction, exposing the machinery of storytelling; the means are the intrusive self-conscious narrator, stories about writing, the reader addressed as reader, and competing endings.
entries.example: If on a winter's night a traveler (Italo Calvino).
entries.application: Any story that knows it is a story; the term is commonly credited to William H. Gass's usage. A writer uses it to make the act of narration part of the subject.

entries.name: The Nouveau Roman
entries.description: Abolishing plot and psychology in favour of surface.
entries.principle: Abolish plot, psychology and the omniscient narrator, presenting surfaces and objects without human-centred meaning; the means are exhaustive object-description, flattened affect, temporal loops, and the refusal of story.
entries.example: Jealousy (Alain Robbe-Grillet).
entries.application: The surface, anti-psychological novel; a writer inherits the possibility of a fiction that describes rather than interprets, its meaning withheld from the human centre.

entries.name: OuLiPo and Constraint
entries.description: Formal constraint as the engine of invention.
entries.principle: Treat constraint not as a limit on creativity but as its engine, so systematic formal rules generate literature; the means are lipograms, mathematical and combinatorial structures, and procedural composition.
entries.example: A Void (Georges Perec), written without the letter e.
entries.application: Procedural and rule-generated fiction. The group is associated with Raymond Queneau and François Le Lionnais around 1960; a writer uses a self-imposed rule to force unforeseen invention.

entries.name: The Encyclopedic / Systems Novel
